frames.narration: A caller searches a graph of 10,000 nodes from node 0. Breadth-first search uses a queue and explores in rings; depth-first search uses a stack and follows one path as far as it goes. With a visited set both do the same work: 19,998 edge checks on a chain, 39,600 on a grid.
The visited set is what makes the search finish. Marking a node when it is first seen, and never listing a marked node again, keeps each node on the waiting list once.

Break it: drop the visited set. On a graph of 100 nodes the search bounces back along the edge it just used and gave up at 100,000 steps. Without any cycle at all, a chain of 20 diamonds costs 2,097,151 node entries instead of 41.

The two searches use memory differently. On a star of 10,000 nodes the BFS queue holds 9,999 nodes at once, while the DFS path is 2 deep. On a binary tree the queue peaks at 5,000 and DFS reaches only 14 deep.

On a chain it is the other way round: the BFS queue never holds more than 1 node, but a recursive DFS needs 10,000 frames. Python's default limit is 1,000, so the recursive version fails. The fix is an explicit stack, which only needs heap memory.
Now the question is the shortest path across a 10,000-node grid. BFS finishes every distance before the next, so its first path to the far corner has 198 edges, the fewest possible.

DFS reaches the far corner after visiting fewer nodes, 9,901 against 10,000, but by a path of 9,900 edges. It finds a path, not the shortest one. Use it for cycle detection, topological order, components and backtracking instead.
